title: Distribution shape, outliers and which average to use
blurb: See how outliers and skew pull the mean but not the median, read a box plot's five-number summary, and choose the right average for the data.
question: Seven ER patients wait 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25 and 180 minutes. The hospital wants one number to describe a typical wait. Should it report the mean or the median, and why?

teach.h: The shape of the data matters
teach.body: Formally, a distribution describes how often each value occurs; its shape can be symmetric or skewed, and an outlier is a value far from the rest. In plain English: picture the data as a pile. If both sides of the pile look alike it's symmetric; if one side trails off into a long tail it's skewed, and the tail drags the mean toward it. That decides which average tells the truth about a 'typical' value.

teach.caption: The hump is on the left, but the long tail runs right, so this is RIGHT (positive) skew. A few huge bills pull the mean above the median.
Skew is named by the TAIL, not by where the hump is.

teach.h: Scenario: Carlos and the ER wait times
items: Carlos Rivera, a nursing applicant shadowing in an ER, records 7 waits: 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25 and 180 minutes.
Mean = 292 ÷ 7 ≈ 41.7 minutes (sum check: 12 + 15 + 18 + 20 + 22 + 25 = 112, plus 180 = 292 ✓). Median = 4th value = 20.
The outlier moved the mean by 23 minutes but the median by just 1. Six of seven patients waited 25 minutes or less, so the median, 20, is the honest 'typical' wait.

teach.caption: The median is RESISTANT to outliers; the mean is not.

teach.h: Measuring spread: range, IQR and standard deviation
teach.body: A box plot shows a five-number summary: minimum, Q1 (first quartile), median, Q3 (third quartile) and maximum. Each section holds about 25% of the data, so the box from Q1 to Q3 is the middle 50%. The interquartile range, IQR = Q3 − Q1, is resistant to outliers; the range (max − min) is not. Standard deviation measures the typical distance from the mean: larger means more spread. On the TEAS, quartiles are given to you, never calculated.

teach.h: A box plot of ER wait times (minutes)
Worked example: reading the box plot
items: Five-number summary: min 5, Q1 12, median 18, Q3 30, max 58.
IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 30 − 12 = 18 minutes (the middle 50% of waits). Range = 58 − 5 = 53 minutes.
Waits longer than 30 minutes (above Q3): about 25% of patients. Waits from 12 to 30 minutes: about 50%.
Shape: the median sits closer to Q1 (6 below it vs 12 above it), and the right whisker (28) is much longer than the left (7). Long right side = right skew, so mean > median.

teach.text: Classic slips: naming skew by the hump ('the bump is on the left, so it's left-skewed'); thinking an outlier moves the median as much as the mean; giving the range when the IQR is asked; and reading the box as the whole data set when it holds only the middle 50%.

items: Outliers pull the mean toward them; the median and IQR barely move.
Right skew: tail to the right, mean > median. Left skew: tail to the left, mean < median.
Skewed data or outliers: report the median. Symmetric: the mean. Categories: the mode.
Box plot: min, Q1, median, Q3, max; each section ≈ 25%; IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Larger standard deviation = more spread around the mean.

summary: You can now tell how an outlier or skew affects the mean and median, name a skew by its tail, read a box plot's five-number summary to find the IQR, range and percentages, and choose the average that honestly describes the data.

A.q: Home sale prices in a county are strongly skewed to the right. Which statement about the prices is most likely correct?
options: The mean is greater than the median
The median is greater than the mean
The mean and median are equal
The mode is greater than the mean
A.why: In a right-skewed distribution a few very high prices form a long right tail, which pulls the mean up above the median.

whyNot.1: The median exceeds the mean in a LEFT-skewed distribution.
whyNot.2: Mean and median are about equal when the data are symmetric.
whyNot.3: In right skew the mode sits at the hump, usually below both the median and the mean.

A.q: Seven nurses worked these overtime hours last month: 4, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 30. If the 30 is removed as an outlier, by how much does the mean decrease? Round to the nearest tenth.
A.why: Mean with the outlier: 70 ÷ 7 = 10. Without it: 40 ÷ 6 = 6.67. Decrease: 10 − 6.67 = 3.33, which rounds to 3.3.

whyNot.0: 0.5 is the change in the MEDIAN (from 7 to 6.5), not the mean.
whyNot.2: 4.3 is 30 ÷ 7: it treats removing the 30 as lowering the mean by 30 shared among 7, but the count also drops to 6.
whyNot.3: 21 is the change in the RANGE (26 to 5), not the mean.

A.q: A box plot of 40 patients' cholesterol levels (mg/dL) shows minimum 142, Q1 168, median 185, Q3 204 and maximum 251. What is the interquartile range?

whyNot.0: 17 is the median minus Q1 (185 − 168), only a quarter of the data.
whyNot.1: 19 is Q3 minus the median (204 − 185), only a quarter of the data.
whyNot.3: 109 is the range (251 − 142), not the interquartile range.

B.q: A small clinic's 12 employees include the physician owner, who earns $480,000 a year; the other 11 earn $38,000 to $72,000. Which measure best describes a typical employee's income?
options: The mean, as it includes every income
The range, as it shows the spread
The midrange of lowest and highest
The median, as it resists the outlier
B.why: The owner's salary is an outlier that drags the mean far above what most employees earn. The median is resistant to outliers, so it shows the typical income.

whyNot.0: Including every income is exactly the problem: the $480,000 outlier pulls the mean far above a typical salary.
whyNot.1: The range measures spread, not a typical value.
whyNot.2: The midrange averages the two extremes, so the outlier distorts it even more than the mean.

B.q: A box plot of 80 applicants' math scores shows minimum 52, Q1 64, median 71, Q3 79 and maximum 94. About how many applicants scored above 79?
B.why: 79 is Q3, so about 25% of the data lie above it. 25% of 80 = 20 applicants.

whyNot.0: 15 is the score gap from Q3 to the maximum (94 − 79), not a number of applicants.
whyNot.2: 40 is half the applicants, the share in the box (Q1 to Q3) or above the median.
whyNot.3: 60 is 75% of 80, the number who scored at or BELOW Q3.

B.q: A box plot of clinic wait times shows minimum 10, Q1 14, median 16, Q3 25 and maximum 48 (minutes). Which best describes the shape of the distribution?
B.why: The median (16) sits close to Q1 (14) and far from Q3 (25), and the right whisker (48 − 25 = 23) is much longer than the left (14 − 10 = 4). The long side is on the right: right skew.

whyNot.0: Left skew would put the long whisker and the wide half of the box on the LEFT.
whyNot.2: A symmetric box plot has the median near the center of the box and whiskers of similar length.
whyNot.3: A bell shape is symmetric; these sections are clearly lopsided to the right.

C.q: The ages of 10 children seen at a pediatric clinic are 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 14 and 15. Which statement is correct?
C.why: Sum = 60, so mean = 60 ÷ 10 = 6. The 5th and 6th values are 4 and 4, so median = 4. Mean > median, with a tail of high values (14 and 15): right skew.

whyNot.1: The numbers are right, but the tail of high ages runs to the right, so the skew is right, not left.
whyNot.2: This swaps the mean and median; the high values pull the mean up to 6.
whyNot.3: 4.5 averages the 6th and 7th values; with 10 values the middle pair is the 5th and 6th (4 and 4).

C.q: Two clinics both have a mean wait time of 20 minutes. Clinic A's standard deviation is 3 minutes and Clinic B's is 11 minutes. Which statement is correct?
options: Clinic A's waits are more spread out
Clinic B's waits are longer on average
Clinic A's waits are shorter on average
Clinic B's waits are more spread out
C.why: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. With equal means, the larger standard deviation (Clinic B's 11 minutes) means more variable waits.

whyNot.0: Clinic A's smaller standard deviation means its waits are MORE consistent, not more spread out.
whyNot.1: Both clinics average 20 minutes; standard deviation describes spread, not the average.
whyNot.2: The means are equal, so neither clinic is shorter on average.

C.q: Nine homes on a street sold for a mean of $255,000 and a median of $240,000. A tenth home then sells for $1,200,000. Which statement is correct?
C.why: Old total = 9 × $255,000 = $2,295,000. New total = $3,495,000. New mean = $3,495,000 ÷ 10 = $349,500, a rise of $94,500. The median only shifts to the average of two middle prices.

whyNot.1: $105,000 divides the $945,000 excess by 9 instead of by the new count, 10.
whyNot.2: The median is resistant: one high sale moves it only to the average of the two middle prices, not by $94,500.
whyNot.3: $945,000 is how far the new sale is above the old mean, not the change in the mean.

reteach.title: A billionaire walks into a coffee shop
reteach.question: Ten people in a coffee shop each earn about $50,000 a year. A billionaire walks in. What happens to the 'average' income in the room?

blocks.h: One person, a very different mean
blocks.body: Before the billionaire arrives, the mean and median are both about $50,000. Afterward the mean is over $90 million, though nobody else got a raise. The median barely moves: it's still roughly $50,000, because it only cares about the middle person in line. That's why news reports use median household income: a few huge values would make the mean misleading.

blocks.text: The tail names the skew: one huge value on the RIGHT makes the data right-skewed, and the mean chases the tail.

explain.body: An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. Because the mean uses every value's size, an outlier pulls it strongly. The median only uses position, so it hardly moves.

test.q: A nurse records the number of call-light requests from 6 patients during a shift: 3, 5, 6, 6, 8 and 40. Which pair gives the mean and median? Round to the nearest tenth.
test.why: Sum = 3 + 5 + 6 + 6 + 8 + 40 = 68; mean = 68 ÷ 6 = 11.3. With 6 values, the median averages the 3rd and 4th: (6 + 6) ÷ 2 = 6.

whyNot.0: 5.6 is the mean with the 40 removed (28 ÷ 5); the question includes all 6 values.
whyNot.1: 7 averages the 4th and 5th values (6 and 8); the middle pair of 6 values is the 3rd and 4th.
whyNot.3: This swaps the two measures; the outlier pulls the mean, not the median, up to 11.3.

explain.body: Skew is named by the long tail. Tail to the right: right (positive) skew, mean > median. Tail to the left: left (negative) skew, mean < median. Symmetric: mean ≈ median.

test.q: On an easy pharmacology quiz, most students scored between 85 and 100, but a few scored below 40, forming a long tail on the left. Which is most likely true?
options: The mean is greater than the median
The mode is less than the mean
The mean is less than the median
test.why: A long left tail is left skew. The few very low scores pull the mean down below the median.

whyNot.0: Mean > median fits a long RIGHT tail.
whyNot.1: Mean and median are about equal only for symmetric data.
whyNot.2: In left skew the mode sits at the hump among the high scores, above the mean.

explain.body: Categories (blood type, reason for visit): mode. Numbers with outliers or skew (incomes, hospital charges): median. Symmetric numbers with no outliers: mean.

explain.h: Match the data to the measure
head: Data
Best center
rows: Most common reason for an ER visit

test.q: An ER manager wants to report the most typical reason patients give for their visit (chest pain, injury, fever, breathing problems and so on). Which measure should she use?
test.why: Reasons for a visit are categories, not numbers. The mode (most frequent category) is the only measure of center that works for categorical data.

whyNot.0: You cannot add and divide categories, so there is no mean reason for a visit.
whyNot.1: Categories have no numerical order, so there is no middle value.
whyNot.3: The range measures numerical spread, not a typical value.

explain.body: A box plot shows the five-number summary. Min to Q1, Q1 to median, median to Q3 and Q3 to max each hold about 25% of the data. IQR = Q3 − Q1, the middle 50%.

test.q: A box plot of resting heart rates has minimum 48, Q1 60, median 66, Q3 75 and maximum 92 beats per minute. About what percent of the patients have a resting heart rate from 60 to 92?
test.why: 60 is Q1, so about 25% of rates are below it. Everything from Q1 to the maximum is the remaining 75%.

whyNot.0: 25% is just one section, such as Q3 to the maximum (75 to 92).
whyNot.1: 50% is the box alone (Q1 to Q3, 60 to 75); the upper whisker adds another 25%.
whyNot.3: 100% runs from the minimum, 48, not from Q1, 60.
